### page_1
Geophys. J. R. astr. SOC. (1983)75, 217-234 
Palaeomagnetism of NW Scotland syenites in relation 
to local and regional tectonics 
H. B. Turnell* and J. @. Briden Department ofEurth Sciences, 
University of Leeds, Leeds LS2 9JT 
Received 1983 February 28; in original form 1982 October 1 I 
Summary. A detailed thermal demagnetization study has been carried out on 
a number of syenitic intrusions from north of the Great Glen Fault in 
Scotland. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have 
been recognized. These define a series of palaeomagnetic poles from which 
an Ordovician to Silurian apparent polar wander path for northern Scotland 
is deduced. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- 
lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and 
magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) 
movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. 
The data emphasize previously published discrepancies between the 
apparent polar wander paths of Britain, Baltica and Laurentia and are con- 
sistent with the suggestion that Britain was among a set of intracratonic 
microplates which underwent complicated, distinct movements throughout 
the Caledonian orogeny. 
1 Introduction 
Lower Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data for Scotland are confined to the Southern Uplands 
and the Highlands between the Highland Boundary and Great Glen Faults while Proterozoic 
data are confined to the Lewisian foreland region. Hence the data distribution is inadequate 
to make a full palaeomagnetic assessment of the amount of relative translation and rotation 
within the region during the Caledonian orogeny. 
Recent studies in the Alpine-Mediterranean region (e.g. Channel1 & Horvith 1976; Edel, 
Montigy & Thuizat 1981) and the North American western cordillera (e.g. Irving 1979; 
Coney, Jones & Monger 1980) have shown that translations and rotations of both large and 
small blocks within orogenic belts are to be anticipated in addition to the large-scale crustal 
shortening brought about by the collision of major plates. 
In the Caledonides, geological evidence (McKerrow & Cocks 1976; Thirlwall 1981) 
supports the existence of an ocean, the Iapetus, between the Southern Uplands and the Lake 
District during the Cambrian and Ordovician which finally closed in late Silurian or early 
Devonian time. Briden, Morris & Piper (1973) attempted to assess the overall amount of 
closure across the Caledonides by comparison of Ordovician palaeomagnetic data from 
England and Wales with that from the Younger Gabbros of Aberdeenshire and estimated 
*Now at: Department of Geology, University College, PO Box 78, Cardiff CPl IXL. 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/75/1/217/613493 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_2
218 H. B. Turnell and J. C. Briden 
post-Ordovician closure as approximately 1000 +/- 800 km while expressing doubts as to 
whether this estimate was significantly different from zero. More recently Deutsch (1 981, 
1982) has suggested post-mid-Ordovician closure of 330 +/-2200 km within Ireland. 
These estimates are unsatisfactory because of the large uncertainties associated with the 
figures. More importantly, this postulated closure across the Iapetus ocean is small compared 
with the discrepancies between these British Ordovician-Silurian data and the contemporary 
North American data on conventional north Atlantic reconstructions (e.g. Bullard, Everett & 
Smith 1965) suggesting that an even larger tectonic discontinuity existed between Britain 
and the North American craton margin. Van der Voo & Scotese (1982) have argued that 
large (- 2000km) post-Caledonian movement along the Great Glen Fault could account for 
these discrepancies. Further, in the Devonian the British data are not only discordant with 
North American data, but also with those from the Baltic region. 
As a contribution to the enhancement of the database, which is a prerequisite to the 
solution of these problems, intrusive rocks in the thrust belt marginal to the deformed 
Caledonides and adjacent to the stable foreland have been studied palaeomagnetically and 
the results are reported in this paper. They have all been regarded as of Ordovician age 
although direct evidence of this is only available for some of them. 
Figure 1. Distribution of the major alkaline intrusions in NW Scotland. The major nappes are also shown 
(after Parsons 1972).

### page_3
Palaeomagnetism of NW Scotland syenites 719 
The main sampling areas of this study are Assynt and Ben Loyal (Fig. 1). The Assynt 
district is centred on a series of thrusted Cambrian sediments between the Lewisian fore- 
land to the west and the Moine schists to the east. The Assynt igneous suite comprises two 
major intrusions, the Borrolan and Loch Ailsh centres (Fig. l), and a complex of dykes and 
sills. The Ben Loyal igneous complex lies some 30 km north of Assynt and intrudes Moine 
metasediments. Additionally, a small collection was made from the Achmelvich dyke 
intruding Lewisian gneisses on the stable Caledonian foreland some 20 km west of Assynt. 
The multicomponent remanences found in these rocks will be discussed in relation to the 
timing and scale of local thrusting as well as in relation to the larger scale plate movements 
associated with Caledonian orogenesis. 
2 Geology 
Almost all the successful palaeomagnetic studies on the Scottish Lower Palaeozoic have been 
made on dioritic, andesitic, basaltic and ultrabasic igneous rocks. Many of the more acid 
rocks are palaeomagnetically unstable, e.g. Newer Granites of Garabal Hill (Briden 1970) and 
Criffel-Dalbeattie (S. J. Kneen, unpublished data). The subjects of the present study are 
mainly alkaline intrusive rocks, although composition varies considerably within and 
between the complexes. Chemical and isotopic age data suggest a genetic relationship to the 
Newer Granite suite (Turnell 1982). 
The position of the intrusions on the different thrust sheets can be seen from the map 
(Fig. 1). The Sole, Ben More, Glencoul and Assynt thrusts form an imbricate series which 
youngs to the west (Elliot & Johnson 1980). The Moine Thrust overrides the other nappes 
from the east and it may be that this difference in geometry of the Moine nappe is related to 
the Assynt intrusions having already been emplaced in the imbricate pile. 
The Borrolan complex (Fig. 2) comprises an outer suite and an inner suite separated by

### page_4
220 
an intrusive junction. The outer suite is subdivided into ledmorite-type exposed in the 
north-west and possibly younger pseudoleucite-type exposed in the south-east. These form 
a conformable sheeted complex which was subsequently punched through by the plug-like 
body of inner syenite. Exposure is poor, especially of the outer phases, for which sampling 
was limited to the river sections, a quarry and isolated exposures in the peaty lowland. A 
total of 21 sites were drilled, of which 10 were in the inner phase (Fig. 2). 
The Loch Ailsh intrusion consists of a variety of broadly uniform leuco-syenites which 
are well exposed, and a total of six sites were drilled. 
Lamprophyric dykes and sills exposed along the road and along the shore of Loch Assynt, 
north of Borrolan, were sampled at nine sites. The Achmelvich dyke was sampled at the 
coast near Lochinver. It is petrographically similar to ledmorite suggesting a common mag 
matic origin (Sabine 1953). 
The Ben Loyal syenite complex comprises three distinct centres of varying grain size and 
composition. The coarse rock of Ben Loyal itself was sampled at one site, eight sites were 
drilled in the finer-grained, most mafic Cnoc nan Cuilean intrusion, including two sites in 
cross-cutting aplite dykes.

3 Method 
Routinely, individual specimens from each site were thermally demagnetized to 700'C 
mainly in steps of 50°C, and in steps of 10-20°C between 450 and 600°C. Another speci- 
men from each site was af demagnetized in steps of 5-lOmT. Only after a definite pattern

### page_5
Palaeomagiietism of NW Scotland syenites 221 
of behaviour had emerged for each site was the rate of experimentation increased by using 
fewer, appropriately chosen temperature and field intervals. 
In general, straight line segments on orthogonal projections of demagnetization data 
define single components of NRM. Although it is often difficult to determine exactly which 
points on a demagnetization trajectory ‘belong’ to a straight line segment, some decision is 
necessary in order to make ‘best estimates’ of the direction of magnetization components 
and of their blocking temperature (or coercivity) ranges. In this study, minimization of the 
95 per cent confidence angle Aa95 on vector differences of Briden & Arthur 1981) 
was used as the criterion. 
Hysteresis and thermomagnetic curves were generated for specimens from each formation 
to provide additional information about the remanence carriers (Fig. 3). 
4 Results 
NRM intensities of all specimens were in the range 10 to 500 x 10-3A m-l with directions 
close to that of the present field. Koenigsberger ratios, Qn, peaked around 0.2 for material 
from the Borrolan outer phase but were more evenly distributed between 0 and 1 .O for the 
rest of the specimen collection. These results indicate the widespread occurrence of coarse- 
grained magnetite. 
Af demagnetization was not generally successful in isolating ancient components of 
magnetization. Most specimens showed erratic directional changes at field strengths greater 
than 20mT. This behaviour is attributed to the high proportion of viscous remanence 
carriers in the rocks which pick up stray fields either in the demagnetizer or during measure- 
ment. Upon thermal treatment, however, a high proportion of specimens showed smooth 
demagnetization trends from which one or more ancient components of magnetization could 
be determined. 
In situ remanence directions identified in the magnetically stable specimens are listed 
with their blocking temperature ranges, in Tables 1-6 and their directions are illustrated in 
Figs 4 and 5. No bedding corrections were applied because there is no evidence that post- 
cooling tilt affected the major intrusions. The remanence directions are labelled N 
(normal) = upward northerly, R (reversed) = downward southerly, or B (downward 
northerly) in the analysis described below. Question marks indicate anomalous components. 
The data are grouped according to formation and, for the Borrolan outer phase, are further 
subdivided into rock-units. Hence, individual specimens are given unit weight in the Fisher 
(1 953) analysis and calculation of mean poles. 
4.1 BORROLAN OUTER PHASE 
Most specimens revealed two components of magnetization (Table 1 and Fig. 5a): a negative 
north-northwesterly component (interpreted as primary, normal magnetization, N) carried 
by magnetite and haematite with blocking temperatures in the range 5O0-69O0C, and a 
south-southeasterly positive component (R) of lower blocking temperature (approximately 
100-500°C) which is interpreted as a later PTRM acquired in a reversed magnetic field 
(e.g. K30-6, Fig. 4a, b). Reversed components were rare at sites B2 and K29. Some of the 
reversed directions had steeper inclinations than the rest of the collection. In the absence 
of any other diagnostic feature they have been included with all the other data from the 
ledmorites in calculating a single palaeomagnetic pole. However, it is possible that these 
steeper directions are composites due to overlap of blocking temperature ranges of shallow 
N and R components. It is also possible that they are younger than the other components 
in these rocks and correlated with reversed magnetization in the inner syenite (see later).

The blocking temperatures and ranges quoted refer 
to the data points between which the removed 
vector has been calculated. They do not, there- 
fore, necessarily cover exactly the total blocking 
temperature range for each component. D, Z 
represent declination ("E of N) and inclination 
(positive downward) of removed vectors during 
progressive demagnetization. Aa,, is the cone of 
95 per cent confidence about that direction 
(Briden & Arthur 1981). The notation N, R, B of 
remanence components is explained in the text. 
Site K31 is the only one from the contact zone between the outer and inner phases. Its 
NRM is unique among the syenite in revealing only a south-easterly positive component 
with a high magnetite blocking temperature. This direction is characteristic of the outer 
phase (Fig. 5a) although the rock specimens are mineralogically similar to the material of the 
inner intrusion. However, the dark, magnetite rich bands observed in thin section may be 
part of the mafic ledmorite and dominate the high temperature remanence. Therefore, the 
results were included in the ledmorite mean. 
The south-eastern pseudoleucites of the Borrolan outer phase were sampled at sites B4, 
in a quarry and B30. Specimens from B4 contained both reversed and normal components 
with blocking temperatures approximately in the ranges 200-500°C and 500-580°C

respectively (Fig. 4a, b and Table 2). Material from site B30 is highly altered although not 
obviously sheared. Over half the specimens appeared to be totally remagnetized by lightning, 
but the remainder contained stable ancient magnetizations, with blocking temperatures 
appropriate to haematite, similar to the high blocking temperature directions in B4. 
4.2 BORROLAN INNER PHASE (SYENITE) 
The directional scatter among primary magnetization directions in the three sites B32, B35 
and K35 is low (Fig. 5b and Table 3), and the inner phase mean, which has a north-easterly 
negative direction, is significantly different from any results from the outer intrusion (Fig. 5f 
and Table 7). Blocking temperature ranges between 500 and 580°C for most specimens 
indicate that they contain a single magnetite ancient remanence, referred to as N magneti- 
zation henceforth. Only one specimen, K35-6, contained a southerly R component with 
blocking temperature around 400"C, interpreted as a later PTRM acquired in a reversed field 
(Fig. 4a). Specimens B35-6B and B32-6 contain evidence of a north-easterly positive 
direction, B, carried by haematite, and magnetite of low blocking temperature, respectively 
(Table 3). 
The remaining sites from the Borrolan inner phase, B11 and K33, were drilled in 
material of slightly different composition. This mineralogical variation is attributed to 
differentiation (Shand 1910; Woolley 1973). Nevertheless, most specimens contained a

north-easterly negative component, N, with blocking temperatures in the range 450-600°C 
as well as a southerly component with lower blocking temperatures (<400"C) which is 
correlated with the reversed magnetization R in site K35 (Table 3 and Fig. 5b). This R 
magnetization has southerly declination and is not perfectly antiparallel to N. It could be 
due to slightly overlapping blocking temperatures of the normal and reversed magneti- 
zations, but we have no direct evidence for this. It could be of significantly different age 
from N. However, so few data are involved that we have calculated their statistics together 
and any distortion due to this procedure is small. The site means of the N component from 
B11 and K33 have slightly lower declination than the other Borrolan syenites but the 
difference is not significant. 
In five out of nine specimens from B11 there is convincing evidence of a north-easterly 
positive remanence, B, with blocking temperature extending into the haematite magneti- 
zation range (Fig. 4a), similar to that seen in B35-6. The origin of the B direction is 
uncertain and these data may be composite vectors resulting from the overlapping blocking 
temperatures of N and R. The presence of haematite is confirmed in the hysteresis curves for 
specimens from Bl l-7 and B35-6 (Fig. 3).

4.3 LOCH AILSH 
NRMs of the Loch Ailsh rocks showed considerable variation (Table 4). Well-defined, multi- 
component remanences were identified in sites B13 to B15, but a large proportion of speci- 
mens from sites B16 and B18 contained only viscous magnetizations (Fig. 4a). Single 
component ancient remanences were determined from a few specimens in these sites but the 
directions were associated with high errors > 20). The hysteresis curve for B18-7 
(Fig. 3) is characteristic of material containing a high proportion of multi-domain titano- 
magnetite. The rocks contained a stable north-easterly negative magnetization (component 
N) similar to the Borrolan inner phase (Fig. 5c). Specimens with the lowest proportion of 
viscous components also contained definite evidence of a lower blocking temperature 
positive north-easterly component, B, of similar direction to that seen in some sites from the 
inner phase of the Borrolan complex. It has the blocking temperature characteristics of a 
later PTRh4 but because of the anomalous direction, satisfactory interpretation requires 
that it be a product of two components, one of which may be the ancient NE upper hemi- 
sphere direction (N). The second component, which may be younger because of the lower 
magnetite blocking temperatures, may have been reversed, or is possibly a recent viscous 
magnetization. In support of the reversed option it is noted that while there were hints of 
reversed components in several specimens especially in the low temperature steps (eg. 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/75/1/217/613493 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_12
228 
186-289°C in B13-2, Fig. 4a) either the inclinations were steep and it was impossible to 
resolve a reversed positive component from a present field direction, or the stable blocking 
temperature range was too short for a reliable estimate. If this is the correct interpretation, 
it is surprising that, from the complete Loch Ailsh collection, there are no clear examples 
of reversed magnetizations in contrast to results from both Borrolan phases. 
Anomalous but stable southerly negative magnetizations are contained in two specimens 
from site B15. 
H. B. Turnell and J. C. Briden

Hence the palaeomagnetic pole (Table 7) is associated with a low agS. Because the dyke is 
less than 6 m wide it is likely to have cooled rapidly through the blocking temperature of the 
titanomagnetic remanence carrier deduced from thermomagnetic and IRM experiments 
(Fig. 3). The data used to calculate the palaeomagnetic pole, then, may not average out 
secular variation. The blocking temperatures are dominantly in the range 500-580°C with 
only one example of a low blocking temperature component (200-400°C) in B20-4 which 
is one of the few specimens containing very little viscous remanence. 
4.5 OTHER DYKES 
Stable specimens from the lamprophyre suite were limited to sites K32 and B29. They were 
considered separately from the Achmelvich dyke because of their different location and 
coarser texture. The Aa,, values quoted for the removed magnetization components (Table 5)

5 Interpretation 
Fig. 6(a) is a plot of the palaeomagnetic south poles determined from each rock unit. By 
comparison with the established lower Palaeozoic APWP for Britain (e.g. Piper 1979; Briden 
& Duff 1981) the magnetizations in these rocks, and perhaps the magmatic activity itself, 
range in age from upper Ordovician to at least late Silurian, and the following order for the 
sequence of intrusions is inferred: Borrolan ledmorites, Borrolan pseudoleucites and Ben 
Loyal, and finally the dykes, the Borrolan syenite and the Loch Ailsh pluton. 
The pole positions thus indicate tectonic rotation and/or continental drift in the 
Ordovician and Silurian. The rate of this movement is uncertain because the precise age 
range is not well determined, but it could have involved phases of rapid movement. 
The 430Ma age determined for the Borrolan outer phase using lead isotopes (van 
Breemen, Aftalion & Johnson 1979) correlates well with the palaeomagnetic pole. Unfor- 
tunately, there are no isotopic data for the other formations, but various authors have 
published ideas on the sequence of intrusive events from detailed petrology and mapping. 
Woolley (1973) suggested that the pseudoleucites were derived from the same magma as

S is number of (specimen) vectors used in the calculation. Rs is the unit vector sum. k is Fisher's 
(1953) precision estimate. is the semi-angle of the cone of 95 per cent confidence about the 
mean direction. 6p, 6m are the semi-axes of the oval of 95 per cent confidence about the mean pole. 
the ledmorites, but it is difficult to determine from geological evidence whether the chemical 
differentiation occurred before the intrusion of the separate groups or after emplacement, 
i.e. in situ. The implication that the igneous activity spanned (say) 20Myr, though the 
inferred ages for poles 5-7 in Table 7 and Fig. 6 are rather younger than most geologists 
would have anticipated, is not unreasonable. However, it is surprising that the intrusion of 
the syenite left no obvious palaeomagnetic imprint on outer phase rocks close to the contact; 
if such an imprint does exist, then it is contained in the R magnetizations in the outer phase 
and has erratic geographic distribution. 
Field evidence indicates that, while the main thrust movements in the Assynt area 
preceded the Borrolan intrusion, small displacements recurred, producing minor shearing and 
faulting (Woolley 1971). These had no discernible effect on the palaeomagnetic record. 
The proximity of poles from the dykes and the syenite indicates that the injection of the 
dykes, which are restricted to the Sole nappe, coincided with the intrusion of the Borrolan 
syenite in spite of their ledmorite affinities. Also, the close agreement between the Borrolan 
syenite pole and that derived from the Loch Ailsh pluton suggests that these were closely 
coeval. In a detailed comparative study of tp geochemistry of rocks from Borrolan and 
Loch Ailsh Parsons (1972) revealed differences which show that they cannot have been 
co-magmatic, although they may have been broadly contemporaneous. In a later paper, 
Parsons (1979) suggested that the Loch Ailsh pluton pre-dated the Assynt thrust, however, 
the palaeomagnetic results do not contain any evidence of a magnetization which could be 
older than that associated with the Borrolan intrusion. It is possible (but unlikely) that the 
palaeomagnetic direction corresponds to a later, post-thrust remagnetization rather than to 
the original cooling of the body. The Loch Ailsh data can be interpreted, as here, without 
invoking any post-cooling movement on the Moine thrust. 
6 Conclusions 
The palaeomagnetic data in this paper are derived from igneous intrusions of a limited age 
range. With the aid of radiometric age data and some evidence on the sequence of magmatic 
activity, the spread of poles can be interpreted as an Apparent Polar Wander Path for late 
Ordovician to Silurian times. To this can be added the poles from the Moines which 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/75/1/217/613493 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_16
232 
Watts (1982) associated with late Caledonian orogeny. Together, these are the poles denoted 
by solid symbols in Fig. 6(a). Also shown in that figure are the published poles from 
Scotland south of the Great Glen. 
Van der Voo & Scotese (1982) have argued for - 2000 km of post-Devonian sinistral 
movement on the Great Glen on the basis of 200 discrepancy between mid and Upper 
Devonian poles from either side of it (the solid and open squares in Fig. 6a). Unless virtually 
the same amount of dextral motion had previously occurred rapidly, close to the Lower/Middle 
Devonian boundary, this same 20" discrepancy should be evident in the Lower Palaeozoic 
data astride the Great Glen. On the basis of visual inspection of Fig. 6(a) this does not 
appear to be so. Both regions seem to have moved in concert, and their apw paths could well 
be identical. 
However, the paths from the two regions would appear to match even better if the poles 
from south of the Great Glen were displaced -14" southward (on the present grid of 
Fig. 6a). This would reconcile the more precise poles from Silurian (? Lower Devonian) 
volcanic and Newer Granites with poles 3,5,6,7 of the present study which we have already 
argued in Section 5 are likely to relate to a rather younger age than the usually assumed 
Ordovician age of those rocks. 
The Ballantrae poles would move to the latitude of pole 2 (Fig. 6a), but without 
necessarily becoming contradictory with poles 1, 2 or 4 because of various uncertainties 
associated with them. Thus on the basis of the data presented here, post-Lower Palaeozoic 
sinistral movement on the Great Glen Fault of up to 1500 km cannot be ruled out - the 
amount depending on the position of the Euler pole which describes the relative rotation. 
Clearly this matter is not settled, although we shall treat it in more detail elsewhere with 
the aid of further currently unpublished data (Briden et al., in preparation). The Lower 
Palaeozoic apw paths from Scotland (Fig. 6a) and England/Wales (Fig. 6b) are not so 
distinct as to enable unequivocal recognition of the Iapetus ocean between these two areas 
or of estimation of its width. However, the Scottish Ordovician poles (Fig. 6a) all lie 
south of the equator while three of the six English poles (Fig. 6b) lie in very low northerly 
latitudes. This could be indicative of an Iapetus ocean - IOOOkm wide in the Ordovician. 
Closure of this ocean could have continued through the Silurian or early Devonian though 
the palaeomagnetic data are too sparse and imprecise to confirm or deny this. Continued 
convergence would be consistent with the idea that the Newer Granites and Old Red 
Sandstone volcanics are associated with continuing subduction of oceanic crust (Thirlwall 
198 1). 
The poles summarized in Fig. 6(a) reinforce the long-recognized discrepancies with the 
North American and Baltic continents. If relative motion along the Great Glen Fault 
accounts for no more than part of the discrepancy with North America, then further 
transcurrent faults remain to be identified. This would be analogous to the situation else- 
where along the North American craton margin where discrepancies between .displaced 
terrains and the craton appear to be taken up on several faults (Kent 1982). While major 
discontinuities such as the Moine Thrust and the Flannan Thrust [recently discovered by 
seismic reflection profiling off NW Scotland (Smythe et al. 198211 could have been the 
sites of some transcurrent movement in early stages of their evolution, the evidence 
presented in this paper strongly suggests that the majority of the 20" discrepancy between 
British and North American data has to be taken offshore of NW Britain and of the North 
American seaboard because the data from Assynt (west of the Moine Thrust) are of more 
British than American affinity. It follows from this that straightforward matching of the 
Scottish Lewisian foreland with the Greenland Archaean as on the Bullard et al. (1965) or 
similar reconstructions is unlikely to be valid. 
The implication of the discrepancy between the British and Baltic data for major 
H. B. Turnell and J. C, Briden 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/75/1/217/613493 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_17
Palaeomagnetism of NW Scotland syenites '33 
Palaeozoic discontinuity in the North Sea (Briden et al. 1973; Van der Voo & Scotese 
1982) remains enigmatic pending unequivocal data of critical ages from Scandinavia. How- 
ever, a picture does seem to be emerging in which Britain, and perhaps neighbouring parts 
of the Caledonian belt, comprised a set of intracratonic microplates and terrains which 
underwent complicated rotations and transcurrent displacement along the belt in the late 
stages of Caledonian orogeny.
